Neonatal body mass in the North American beaver (Castor canadensis) has been reported from field studies of captive colonies, with newborns weighing approximately 430 grams [Wwb = approximately 430 grams]. This relatively large birth mass for a rodent is consistent with a precocial developmental strategy, as kits are born fully furred with their eyes open and are capable of swimming within their first day of life. The species' extended gestation period of 128 days [tg = 128 days], measured under thermoneutral conditions at a core body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], is notably long among rodents and reflects the advanced state of development attained in utero. Lasting just over four months, this interval encompasses substantial organogenesis and growth, preparing the neonate for a semi-aquatic existence almost immediately after parturition. The timing of parturition itself is often synchronized with the onset of spring thaw in northern latitudes, ensuring that abundant forage is available for the lactating female. Female beavers typically produce a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], and each litter contains approximately 3.5 pups [N_R_i = each litter contains approximately 3.5 pups], a value documented under captive conditions at the standard physiological temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This annual reproductive output is relatively modest compared to many other rodent species, reflecting the beaver's K-selected life-history strategy characterized by high parental investment and extended offspring care.

Weaning in Castor canadensis occurs after a relatively short period of maternal dependency, with kits transitioning to solid food at approximately 14 days [tx = approximately 14 days] after birth, under the same thermoneutral conditions of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This early weaning time (14 days) [tx = 14 days] is facilitated by the precocial nature of the young, which are able to consume tender aquatic vegetation and bark soon after birth, supplementing the milk provided by the dam at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. The rapid onset of independent feeding is critical for the colony's survival, as it allows the mother to focus her energetic resources on maintaining her own body condition and preparing for the next breeding season. Following weaning, the growing juveniles remain within the family unit, learning essential dam-building and foraging skills from their parents and older siblings. Female beavers attain their ultimate adult body mass of 20000 grams [Wwi = 20000 grams], though considerable individual variation exists in this parameter, with literature records ranging from 11000 to 32000 grams. This large adult size, among the largest of all rodents, is a key adaptation for their semi-aquatic lifestyle, providing thermal inertia in cold water and the physical strength necessary to fell trees and construct lodges.

Sexual maturation in the North American beaver is a protracted process compared to the rapid developmental milestones of early life. Puberty, defined as the age at which individuals first become capable of reproduction, occurs at 639 days [tp = 639 days] after birth under thermoneutral conditions of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This time since birth at puberty (639 days) [tp = 639 days] corresponds to approximately 1.75 years, meaning that beavers typically do not breed until their second or third calendar year of life in the wild at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This extended period of juvenile development is unusual among rodents and is linked to the complex social structure of beaver colonies, where younger animals often serve as helpers before dispersing to establish their own territories. The lengthy interval between weaning and reproductive maturity allows ample time for the acquisition of critical foraging and engineering skills, as well as the accumulation of sufficient body reserves to survive the winter and successfully rear a litter. During this sub-adult phase, individuals continue to grow, gradually approaching the asymptotic body mass that characterizes breeding adults. The social structure of the colony, typically consisting of a monogamous breeding pair and their offspring from one or more years, reinforces the selective pressure for delayed reproduction, as competition for breeding opportunities is intense.

Longevity records for Castor canadensis indicate that this species possesses an exceptionally long lifespan for a rodent of its size. The maximum recorded lifespan under field conditions is approximately 23.4 years [am = approximately 23.4 years], measured at the species' thermoneutral temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. Such an extended longevity is remarkable among rodents, more typical of larger mammals such as ungulates or small carnivores, and is made possible by the beaver's protected lifestyle within stable family groups and lodges, which dramatically reduces predation risk compared to smaller, solitary rodents. Additionally, their large body size and low mass-specific metabolic rate contribute to a slower pace of life, characterized by delayed reproduction, extended parental care, and reduced annual reproductive output. The combination of these life-history traits aligns with predictions from metabolic theory, which posits that larger-bodied organisms with lower mass-specific metabolic rates tend to exhibit longer lifespans and slower life histories. In the absence of significant predation pressure from wolves or bears, and with access to abundant food resources, individuals can attain ages that far exceed the typical rodent ceiling of three to five years.

Basal metabolic rate in Castor canadensis has been measured directly via respirometry trials on captive animals. At a core body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], the maximum basal oxygen consumption recorded in this species is 4688 milliliters per hour [JOi = 4688 milliliters per hour]. This metabolic rate of 4688 milliliters per hour [JOi = 4688 milliliters per hour] is substantial in absolute terms but, when expressed on a mass-specific basis, is relatively low for a mammal of its body size, consistent with the energetically conservative lifestyle of a large, semi-aquatic herbivore at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. The measured value aligns well with allometric predictions for a rodent of approximately 20 kilograms, falling close to the 0.75 power scaling relationship that characterizes mammalian basal metabolism. The low mass-specific metabolic rate of beavers is an important adaptation for their semi-aquatic lifestyle, as it reduces the energetic cost of maintaining body temperature in cold water. Furthermore, this conservative metabolic strategy allows beavers to subsist on a diet of bark and aquatic vegetation that is relatively low in digestible energy content. The combination of large body size, low metabolic rate, and efficient digestive physiology enables beavers to thrive in boreal and temperate ecosystems where food quality is seasonally variable.
